claims.text: Heavy alcohol consumption monotonically increases the relative risk of hemorrhagic stroke.
Alcohol consumption exhibits a curvilinear J-shaped dose-response relationship with the relative risk of ischemic stroke.
Low to moderate alcohol consumption is associated with a protective effect against ischemic stroke.
For women, the relative risk of alcohol consumption on stroke differs significantly when comparing mortality endpoints to morbidity endpoints.

evidence.description: At 96 g/day of pure alcohol (8 US standard drinks), relative risks for hemorrhagic stroke mortality were 1.94 (95% CI: 1.56-2.40) for men and 4.50 (95% CI: 2.47-8.20) for women compared to lifetime abstainers.
Ischemic stroke risk showed a J-shaped curve for both mortality and morbidity across sexes, with decreased risk at low doses and increased risk at high doses.
For men, alcohol consumption of 12 g/day (1 drink/day) achieved a global minimum relative risk of 0.86 (95% CI: 0.81-0.93) for ischemic stroke mortality relative to lifetime abstainers.
The interaction term between endpoint type (mortality vs morbidity) and alcohol dose was statistically significant for women in both hemorrhagic stroke (p = 0.0138) and ischemic stroke (p = 0.0141).

methodologies.name: Systematic review and random-effects meta-regression with fractional polynomials
methodologies.description: A systematic literature search across 8 databases followed by random-effects meta-regression using fractional polynomials to model dose-response curves for stroke risk stratified by stroke type, sex, and outcome.
conditions: Stratification by stroke subtype (ischemic vs hemorrhagic)
Stratification by endpoint outcome (morbidity vs mortality)

limitations.text: Previous meta-analyses on alcohol and stroke focused primarily on stroke mortality and failed to explicitly differentiate between morbidity and mortality outcomes.
Some primary studies lacked CT scans or imaging diagnostic techniques, relying instead on death certificates, registry data, or autopsy reports to classify stroke subtypes.
Primary data relied on self-reported alcohol consumption, which is subject to recall bias and underreporting by heavy drinkers.
Adjusting current abstention reference groups to lifetime abstention required pooling former-drinker ratios across fatal and non-fatal outcomes combined, which may introduce minor bias.

future_work.text: Initiate public health alcohol control measures to mitigate projected global increases in alcohol-attributable stroke burden.
Evaluate public health guidelines recommending limiting alcohol consumption to 2 or fewer drinks per day to maintain potential cardio-protective benefits while minimizing stroke risk.
